title: The divine image
hookLine: Mercy, Pity, Peace and Love dwell in the human form, and where they dwell, God dwells too (The Divine Image)
tomorrow: how do you hold on to a joy without crushing it?

cards: When the news is bad, people share small clips: a stranger carrying someone's groceries up the stairs, a nurse singing to a patient. The comments often say the same thing: faith in humanity, restored.

Blake wrote a poem about where that feeling points. It's called The Divine Image, and it starts with what people turn to when they're in trouble: "To Mercy Pity Peace and Love, / All pray in their distress".
So where do those four live?

teach.b: Blake's answer: "For Mercy has a human heart / Pity, a human face: / And Love, the human form divine, / And Peace, the human dress."

The poem says the human form must be loved in everyone, whatever their faith, and it ends: "Where Mercy, Love & Pity dwell, / There God is dwelling too." That's Blake's Christian answer, rooted in yesterday's teaching.
On that reading, if God became a little child, the human form has become a place where God can be found. Now a neighbor's version, in its own words.

teach.h: TZELEM ELOHIM: THE IMAGE OF GOD.
teach.b: Judaism teaches it from the Bible's first chapter: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him". In Hebrew, tzelem Elohim. The Mishnah tells it as a picture.

A human king stamps coins from one seal, and they all come out alike. God stamped every person with the seal of the first human, and not one is like another. So every face carries the image, and every face is different.
That's what the two share: the human face as a place to meet the holy, and so a reason to treat every person with dignity. And the honest difference.
For Blake, Love is the human form divine, and behind it stands Christ, God made flesh. Jewish teaching keeps God beyond any form.

teach.h: YE SAW NO MANNER OF FORM.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb, the mountain of God, "ye saw no manner of form", and so no image of God is made.
In that teaching, the image is in us; God isn't shaped like us.

how: Jewish teaching holds that every person is created b'tzelem Elohim, in God's image, and make no image of God; Christians speak of the human person as God's image renewed in Christ, and The Divine Image is sung as a hymn in some churches.

at Horeb ye saw no manner of form, Deuteronomy says, and no image of God is made.

games.q: a Jewish friend and a Christian friend both say every person bears God's image. what's the honest difference today named?
o: for Blake, Love is the human form divine, through Christ; Jewish teaching keeps God beyond any form.
they mean exactly the same thing, so there's no difference worth naming at all.
Judaism teaches people are divine, while Christianity teaches people are only dust.
games.why: both see the image of God in every face. Blake's human form divine rests on God made flesh in Christ; Jewish teaching says God has no form, and no image of God is made.

practice: Bring one person to mind, and count the four off on your fingers: where have you seen their mercy, their pity, their peace, their love? Take two minutes, one finger at a time, and give thanks for each, to God or to them.

wordCard.voice: The divine image: Blake's song that God dwells where mercy, pity, peace and love dwell, in a human heart, face, form and dress.

orig.note: Hebrew: the image of God, from Genesis 1:27; the Jewish teaching that every person bears it.

carryVoice: Carry this: mercy, pity, peace, love, each one wearing a human face, and God dwelling there too. Almost there.
